For Fair Work purposes, from 26 August 2024 companies use the whole of relationship test, which looks at the real substance, practical reality and true nature of the working relationship. Sham contracting penalties apply to a business that tells an employee they are a contractor, unless it proves it reasonably believed they were one.

final.after: Only if more tax was withheld across the year than you owe on your actual taxable income. On a normal termination your employer uses the ATO's marginal rate method in Schedule 7: the payout is divided across a full year of pay periods (52 weekly, 26 fortnightly or 12 monthly), the extra tax on one share is worked out from the normal tax table, and that amount is multiplied back up. Employees with redundancy may receive concessional treatment on certain payments, but the annual leave component itself remains fully taxable.
final.after: If you resign, retire or are dismissed, unused annual leave and leave loading that accrued on or after 18 August 1993 are taxed at your marginal tax rate. Any part that accrued before 18 August 1993 is withheld at {pc(TERMINATION_LOADING_WITHHOLDING.flatRate)}. If you leave because of a genuine redundancy, invalidity or an early retirement scheme, your employer withholds {pc(TERMINATION_LOADING_WITHHOLDING.flatRate)} of the whole unused annual leave and leave loading payment, whatever date it accrued.

final.before: Salary sacrifice specifically refers to redirecting pre-tax salary into superannuation. All salary sacrifice is salary packaging, but not all salary packaging is salary sacrifice.
final.after: They are the same arrangement. The ATO says salary sacrificing is also known as salary packaging or total remuneration packaging: you agree to take less pre-tax salary and your employer pays for benefits of similar value instead. The benefits can be extra super contributions, a novated car lease, a work-related laptop and, at some not-for-profit employers, living expenses and meal entertainment. What changes from one benefit to another is the FBT treatment, not the name.
final.quote: Salary sacrificing is also known as salary packaging or total remuneration packaging. ... There is no restriction on the types of benefits you can include in a salary sacrifice arrangement.
final.note: Checked against the cached ATO page (last updated 11 August 2026). The new answer matches the ATO wording. The question text is unchanged and there are no dashes or new hedging.

final.before: Private sector employees cannot access these caps. Their packaging options are limited to super, novated leases, and portable devices.
final.after: Private sector employees cannot access these caps. They can still package super, a novated car lease and FBT-exempt work-related items such as a laptop. Other benefits can be packaged too, but the employer pays FBT on them unless an exemption applies.
final.quote: There is no restriction on the types of benefits you can include ... Your employer will have to pay fringe benefits tax (FBT) on the value of the benefit ... Your employer won't have to pay FBT on exempt work-related items, such as a portable electronic device
final.note: The ATO page proves this. Work-related items are exempt in the current FBT year, which ends 31 March 2027. The 1 April 2027 change is covered in FAQ 46 and in the body.

The device must be used mainly (more than 50%) for employment duties. From 1 April 2027, work-related items provided through salary sacrifice are no longer exempt from FBT, so a device packaged from that date attracts FBT.

final.before: Salary sacrifice specifically refers to redirecting pre-tax salary into superannuation. Salary packaging encompasses the full range of benefits an employer can provide from pre-tax earnings. The distinction matters because different benefits have different FBT treatment, caps, and eligibility rules.
final.after: The ATO places no restriction on the types of benefits you can include, as long as they form part of your pay and replace salary you would otherwise receive. What differs between benefits is the FBT treatment, the caps and the eligibility rules.

calculateSchedule5MethodB is labelled 'Method B(ii)', but its steps are the ATO's Method A. It uses the current period's regular gross, divides by the pay periods in the year, takes the difference, multiplies back and caps at 47%. ATO Method B(ii) instead uses 'average total earnings ... over the current financial year to date' and adds earlier B(ii) payments, then subtracts amounts already withheld. The output is a valid ATO method ("Calculations made using either method are acceptable"), so the figures are not wrong. Only the name and doc comment are. Proposed change (owner of payg-withholding.ts): change the comment/section header to 'Schedule 5, Method A'. Renaming the function is an engine change that needs a decision. No change made.
